claims.text: Above 900 °C, a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide forms on CrFeCoNiX only when X is Si.
Si promotes formation of a continuous interfacial oxide phase.
The Si-promoted interfacial phase minimizes thermal-expansion mismatch.
Minimizing thermal-expansion mismatch inhibits crack initiation in the oxide scale.
Mn- and Al-containing variants form thicker oxides than the Si-containing alloy.
Oxides on Mn- and Al-containing variants are mechanically unstable and prone to cracking or spallation.
A beneficial interfacial phase, such as a glassy Si-rich layer, mediates formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale.
Si may enhance chromium enrichment within the oxide scale.
Si may nucleate a glassy phase within the oxide scale.
The dense Si-associated interfacial oxide reduces interfacial stress.
Reduced interfacial stress suppresses crack development.
Mn- or Al-containing alloys do not promote the proposed beneficial interfacial phase.
Si-containing alloys will retain an intact, uniform, adherent oxide during prolonged exposure above 900 °C.
Si-containing alloys will exhibit slower oxide growth than Mn- or Al-containing controls.
Mn- and Al-containing alloys provide a controlled baseline expected to form less coherent and less stable oxide scales under identical exposure conditions.
The proposed behavior applies to single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres above 900 °C.
Substantially different reactive species, temperatures, or alloy microstructures may change the oxidation behavior.
Failure of the Si-containing alloys to show statistically significant improvements in oxide coherence, growth rate, and adhesion over both controls would falsify the hypothesis.
